question: The double-slit experiment: how can single particles make stripes?

research.claim: Quantum particles sent through two slits one at a time each arrive as a single localized dot, yet the distribution of many arrivals shows interference stripes. The probability of landing at a point is the squared magnitude of an amplitude that is the sum of contributions through both slits; where the two contributions are out of phase they cancel and almost no particles land, even at spots that receive particles when only one slit is open. Closing a slit, or determining which slit each particle passed, removes the stripes.
research.explanation: In the double-slit experiment a source sends particles toward a barrier with two narrow slits and a screen behind it. With the rate low enough that only one particle is in the apparatus at a time, each detection is a single point on the screen: the particle is never found spread out or split. Where any one particle lands is random. With one slit open, many arrivals build a single broad patch. With both open, the arrivals build bands of many hits separated by bands with almost none. Quantum mechanics describes each particle with a wave of probability amplitude that passes through both slits; the two parts overlap, and the chance of detection at each point is the squared size of their sum, so it is high where they arrive in step and near zero where they arrive half a wavelength out of step. Because amplitudes add before squaring, opening the second slit lowers the count at the dark bands below the one-slit count. Covering a slit leaves only one contribution, so nothing cancels and the stripes vanish; so does any measurement that records which slit each particle used. Thomas Young described the experiment with light in 1801; Claus Jönsson did it with electrons in 1961; Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi showed single electrons building up the pattern in 1974 (with an electron biprism), and Frabboni and colleagues showed the single-electron build-up through two slits in 2012. Davisson–Germer and Thomson confirmed electron waves in 1927. The effect has since been seen with atoms, C60 molecules and, in 2019, molecules of about 2,000 atoms.
assumptions: An idealised two-slit setup with a broad single-slit envelope and two equal slits; the picture's pattern is the envelope times 1 + a² + 2a cos(phase).
Each dot is a pseudo-random sample from the predicted probability pattern, not a simulated trajectory.
No which-path detector is present, except where the narration says a slit is covered.
The particle type is generic; electrons, photons, atoms and molecules all show it, with different wavelengths.
research.prediction: With both slits open, thousands of single arrivals form stripes whose dark bands receive fewer hits than the same spots receive with one slit open; with one slit closed, the arrivals form a single patch.
research.falsifier: If single-particle arrivals with both slits open simply added up the two one-slit patterns, with no dark bands below the one-slit level, the wave description would be wrong.
limitations: The waves drawn depict the probability amplitude, not a path; the picture never shows which slit a particle used.
The one-slit pattern is drawn centred like the two-slit envelope, a simplification for close slits.
Particle wavelengths, detector efficiency and decoherence are not modelled.
misconceptions: Each particle splits in two: it is always detected whole, in one place.
The stripes come from particles bumping into each other: they appear even when only one particle is in the apparatus at a time.
Watching which slit only disturbs the stripes a little: full which-path information removes them.
questions: Does each particle split in two?
Why does a second slit leave some spots emptier?
What happens if you detect which slit was used?

scene.title: The double-slit experiment: how can single particles make stripes?
scene.subtitle: Fire particles one at a time at a wall with two slits. Each lands as a single dot, yet thousands of dots build up stripes, because each particle passes through the slits as a wave.
scene.why: Electrons, atoms and molecules fired one at a time still build up stripes. Each lands as a dot, but before it lands it spreads like a wave through both slits.
scene.opening: If particles go through the slits one by one, where do the stripes come from?

beats.title: One at a time
beats.body: Imagine a gun that fires tiny particles, one at a time. Each goes through a slit in a wall and hits a screen. It lands as a single dot.

beats.title: Thousands of dots
beats.body: Keep firing, thousands of times. With one slit open, they pile up in one soft patch. The bars on the right count where they land.

beats.title: Open the second slit
beats.body: Now slide the cover off the second slit. Again, each particle lands as one dot. At first, the dots look scattered at random.

beats.title: Stripes appear
beats.body: After thousands more dots, stripes appear. Between the stripes are gaps where almost none land. One slit alone sent dots there; the second slit took them away.

beats.title: A wave through both slits
beats.body: On its way, each particle acts like a spreading wave. The wave goes through both slits and takes two paths to each spot. Where crest meets crest, dots pile up; crest on trough, none land.

beats.title: Close a slit
beats.body: Now cover the second slit, clear the screen and fire again. With one way through, there is nothing to cancel: no stripes. Electrons, atoms and even big molecules all behave this way.

scene.takeaway: Each particle lands as one dot, but where it can land is set by a wave that passes through both slits. Where the two parts of the wave cancel, no particle lands, so stripes build up.

questions.q: Does each particle split in two?
questions.a: No. Each one is always found as one whole dot on the screen. What spreads through both slits is the wave that sets where it may land.

questions.q: Why do the dots look random at first?
questions.a: Each landing spot is a matter of chance. Only the odds are fixed, and the odds show up once thousands of dots have landed.

questions.q: Why does opening a second slit leave some spots empty?
questions.a: There the wave from one slit arrives out of step with the wave from the other, and they cancel, so the chance of landing there drops to almost zero.

questions.q: What if you watch which slit each particle goes through?
questions.a: Then the stripes disappear and the dots pile up as if from two single slits. Knowing the path removes the overlap of the two waves.

questions.q: Has this really been done one particle at a time?
questions.a: Yes. Electrons were shown building up stripes one by one in 1974 and again in 2012, and molecules of up to 2,000 atoms have shown stripes too.

physics_review.summary: Round 2 fixes every round-1 point: in chapter 6 the slit is covered, the screen is cleared and a new one-slit patch builds from zero, so no landed dot moves; chapter 3 no longer shows the readout; the chapter 5 lines describe the wave taking two paths and crest/trough cancellation, a fair simplification that never says the particle splits or takes one path; the research record names Frabboni et al. (2012) and the 1974 biprism, matching the saved source. All dates (1801, 1961, 1974, 2012, 1927, 2019, about 2,000 atoms), readouts and the dashed one-slit comparison are correct and match the frames.
changes: Optional: use 'almost none' in both chapter 4 and chapter 5.
Optional: 'is described by a spreading wave' would hedge the interpretation further; the Q&A already makes the distinction.

visual_review.summary: The 'one slit' pill now sits on the darker dashed curve, chapter 2 fills to a broad single patch, the waves fade before the edges, the COVERED label makes the shutter clear, and chapter 6 holds the closed slit and refills as one patch, so the picture matches the text to the end. Stripes and gaps are very clear on desktop and phone, labels stay few and short, and nothing important is clipped.
changes: Nudge the 'one slit' pill clear of the bar tips.
Hide the first wavelet ring until it clears the wall.
Optional: plainer name for the 'Stripe contrast' readout.

learner_review.summary: My explanation: on its way, each particle acts like a wave that goes through both slits, so two parts of the wave reach every spot by two different paths. Where they arrive high-on-high they add up and dots pile up, and where high meets low they cancel and no dot lands, so thousands of single dots build stripes with gaps. Chapter 5 now gives the cause, chapter 6 matches the picture, and the cover is named. All lines are under 80 characters and read naturally aloud.
changes: Ch5: say the two paths have different lengths.
Ch5: 'crest' and 'trough' could be defined or replaced with high/low.
Ch6: 'nothing cancels, so no stripes' reads better aloud than the colon.
Hide or rename the 'Stripe contrast' badge in chapters 5 and 6.

blind_review.summary: Blind reading: a source fires particles one at a time through one open slit (the other COVERED), each landing as a dot; 2400 build one broad patch; with the cover gone a few dots look random; 2400 form about seven bands with gaps, with a dashed one-slit curve for comparison; waves spread from the source and through both slits; then one slit is covered again and the cleared screen refills as one broad patch. All six chapters match the intended story.
changes: Chapter 6's refilled patch looks identical to chapter 2's; a different random seed would avoid looking reused.
Small wavelet fragments sit inside the slit gaps in chapter 5.
